stances.claim: CJ Gesmundo's motu proprio investigation into the Agbayani lawyer's lapses under the CPRA is laudable, but it falls short of what the family yearns for: a reversal of Agbayani's conviction and a judicial pronouncement of his innocence -- which cannot be taken motu proprio because the offended party (Hofileña) equally deserves objective justice.

The family should initiate a petition, with due notice to Hofileña and to the OSG (counsel of the plaintiff People of the Philippines), to reopen the case -- the overarching question being whether a decision that has become final AND executed can be reopened.

The general rule is that final decisions are irrevocable despite occasional errors -- but several 'final and irrevocable' judgments have in fact been revoked, most glaringly the SBN Pamaran Dec 2, 1985 acquittal of Fabian Ver and others for the Ninoy Aquino murder, which Cory Aquino's SC reopened, found to be a 'sham' trial, and replaced with the Hermosisima 177-page conspiracy conviction of 16 accused-soldiers.
stances.rhetorical_move: exceptional-precedent catalog with the Aquino case as flagship example

stances.claim: More common than acquittal-to-conviction reopenings are conviction-to-acquittal reopenings -- DNA-based exonerations of rape convicts when semen DNA belongs to another man being the canonical modern example.

The writ of habeas corpus, though not normally used to free those detained under valid court orders, has been allowed where the ordering court (1) lacked jurisdiction, (2) imposed an excessive penalty, or (3) deprived the accused of constitutional rights -- a three-exception framework that creates pathways to reopen final convictions.

The Supreme Court is both a court of law and a court of equity -- rules of procedure should never be used as stumbling blocks to common sense, fairness, and equity. The Court is a dispenser of liberating justice, not suffocating rules; neither a machine nor a robot; human and humane; and because it is compassionate and just, it cannot be replaced by the computing power of technology and artificial intelligence.
stances.confidence: asserted as the column's closing thesis

notable_anecdotes: The Agbayani saga in numbers -- MeTC conviction, RTC denial, CA denial, SC-Third Division denial, ALL on the same procedural ground (lawyer's failure to file appeal memorandum and append required documents), followed by Agbayani's death from a heart attack while incarcerated -- the cumulative tragedy of procedural failure compounded across four court tiers.

CJ Gesmundo's Dec 13 press-briefing quote -- 'we may establish new instructions or new rules so that we can avoid a repeat of the same situation... apparently there were some lapses committed by the lawyer' -- used to frame the SC's institutional response.

The Pamaran-acquittal-reopening -- the canonical Philippine example of a 'final and irrevocable' judgment being revoked, with the SBN's Dec 2, 1985 acquittal of Ver and others for the Aug 21, 1983 Ninoy Aquino murder reopened by Cory Aquino's SC in 1986 and replaced by Hermosisima's 177-page retrial conviction of 16 accused-soldiers including Brig. Gen. Luther Custodio.

Fabian Ver as the one who escaped -- indicted but 'could not be included in the guilty verdict because he fled the country, could not be served with court processes, and was therefore beyond the local courts' jurisdiction' -- the residual injustice within the reopened-justice story.
DNA evidence as the canonical modern reopening -- 'the semen found inside the vagina of the victim belonged to a man other than the accused' -- the precision of forensic-science vindication.

The closing anti-AI thesis -- 'It is neither a machine nor a robot. It is human and humane. Being compassionate and just, it cannot be replaced by the computing power of technology and artificial intelligence' -- the strongest CJ statement on the limits of judicial automation, embedded in the equity-vs-rules argument.

one_paragraph_summary: Continuing the sad saga of Dr. Iggy Agbayani -- taken up Nov 13 and followed by CPRA columns Nov 27 and Dec 4 -- Panganiban reports that on Dec 13, 2023, CJ Alexander G. Gesmundo said in a press briefing that the justices will review what happened and may establish new instructions because 'apparently there were some lapses committed by the lawyer.' Agbayani -- a respected orthopedic surgeon convicted by the MeTC of Manila of 'reckless imprudence resulting in serious physical injuries' -- had his appeals denied at the RTC, CA, and SC-Third Division on the same procedural ground: his lawyer's failure to file an appeal memorandum and to append documents required by the Rules of Court. Agbayani died of a heart attack while incarcerated. Under the CPRA, the Court can motu proprio discipline the lawyer -- but, laudable as that is, it falls short of what the family yearns for: a reversal of conviction and a judicial pronouncement of innocence, which cannot be motu proprio because the offended party (Atty. Saul Q. Hofileña Jr.) equally deserves objective justice. CJ recommends the family initiate a petition to reopen the case, with due notice to Hofileña and the OSG. The overarching question is whether a decision that has become final AND executed via incarceration can be reopened. The normal jurisprudential answer is no -- but several 'final and irrevocable' judgments have been revoked. The most glaring example: Justice Manuel Pamaran's Dec 2, 1985 SBN decision acquitting Fabian Ver and other accused of the daring broad-daylight murder of Sen. Ninoy Aquino at the Manila International Airport tarmac on Aug 21, 1983. After Cory Aquino took over in 1986, the SC reopened the verdict, found the trial to be a 'sham,' and authorized a retrial. Justice Regino C. Hermosisima Jr.'s 177-page decision found conspiracy among 16 accused-soldiers including Brig. Gen. Luther Custodio and convicted them of the double murder of Ninoy and Rolando Galman; only Ver escaped conviction by fleeing the country and remaining beyond local jurisdiction. The more common reopenings are convictions later reversed on subsequent proof of impossibility of guilt -- most famously rape convictions overturned by DNA evidence showing the semen belonged to another man. The extraordinary writ of habeas corpus has also been allowed where the ordering court (1) lacked jurisdiction, (2) imposed an excessive penalty, or (3) deprived the accused of constitutional rights. CJ concludes that the Supreme Court is both a court of law and a court of equity. Rules of procedure should never be used as stumbling blocks to common sense, fairness, and equity. The Court cannot be constrained by technicalities and procedural niceties. It is a dispenser of liberating justice, not of suffocating rules. It is neither a machine nor a robot. It is human and humane. Being compassionate and just, it cannot be replaced by the computing power of technology and artificial intelligence.
